title: THEY HAD MANY WIVES. SO WHY CAN’T CHRISTIANS TODAY? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH THAT CHANGES EVERYTHING
paragraphs: THEY HAD MANY WIVES. SO WHY CAN’T CHRISTIANS TODAY? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH THAT CHANGES EVERYTHING

Abraham had Sarah and Hagar. Jacob had Leah and Rachel. David had multiple wives. Solomon had hundreds. But when Jesus spoke about marriage, He took His listeners somewhere they never expected—back before the kings, before the patriarchs, before the heartbreak. And what He revealed should make every Christian reconsider the difference between what God permitted in a fallen world and what God intended from the beginning.
There is a question that can make an entire church uncomfortable.
Not because the Bible refuses to answer it.
But because the Bible contains stories that seem, at first glance, to support the very thing many Christians condemn.
If Abraham, Jacob, David, and Solomon had multiple wives, why do Christians insist that marriage should be between one man and one woman?
Think about that.
These were not obscure men hiding in the shadows of biblical history.
Abraham was called God's friend.
Jacob became the father of the twelve tribes of Israel.
David was described as a man after God's own heart.
Solomon was given extraordinary wisdom.
And yet their households included multiple wives, concubines, rivalry, jealousy, and complicated family relationships.
So here is the uncomfortable question.
If God worked through these men, does that mean He approved of everything they did?
And if the Old Testament records polygamy without always explicitly condemning it, can a Christian today point to those examples and declare, "God allowed it then, so He must allow it now"?
Before you answer, consider something that might change the way you read your Bible forever.
Not everything Scripture records is something Scripture recommends.
The Bible tells us that David committed adultery and arranged a man's death. It does not invite us to imitate him.
It tells us that Abraham lied about Sarah. It does not turn dishonesty into righteousness.
It tells us that Peter denied Jesus three times. It does not make denying Christ acceptable.
And it tells us that men had multiple wives.
But does the existence of those marriages establish God's original design?
That is where this story becomes far more personal than a debate about ancient households.
Because underneath the question about polygamy lies a question every Christian must eventually face.
Are we searching Scripture to discover what God desires?
Or are we searching Scripture for someone whose behavior can justify what we already want?
That question does not belong only to people defending polygamy.
It belongs to the person excusing bitterness because someone in the Bible became angry.
To the person justifying dishonesty because a biblical hero once lied.
To the believer who keeps returning to a destructive relationship because they can find a verse that seems to make it acceptable.
And to every one of us who has ever whispered, "But Lord, someone else did it."
The Gospel does not call us to imitate every failure of the people God used.
It calls us to follow the Savior who came to redeem people like them.
And people like us.
To understand this, we have to return to a place older than Abraham.
Older than Jacob.
Older than David.
Older than the entire nation of Israel.
We have to return to the garden.
Before sin fractured human relationships, before jealousy entered marriage, before powerful men accumulated wives as signs of wealth or status, Scripture introduces a man and a woman.
Adam and Eve.
Not Adam and several wives.
Not Eve competing with another woman for her husband's attention.
One man.
One woman.
One covenantal union.
Genesis 2:24 declares:
"Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh." (KJV)
The Hebrew text contains the expression:
וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
Ve-hayu le-vasar echad.
"And they shall become one flesh."
The word echad means "one."
In this context, the phrase describes the profound union established through marriage.
It is not merely about physical intimacy.
It is about two lives joined in a covenantal bond.
We should be careful not to claim that the Hebrew word echad, by itself, proves monogamy. Hebrew can use this word in several ways, and the meaning must be determined by context.
But the context matters enormously.
Genesis presents one man joined to his wife, and the two becoming one flesh.
And centuries later, when Jesus was questioned about marriage, He deliberately returned to this passage.
That should get our attention.
Because when people challenged Jesus about the boundaries of marriage, He did not begin with Solomon's household.
He did not point to Jacob's arrangements.
He did not make David's royal marriages the controlling example.
He went back to creation.
In Matthew 19:4–6, Jesus said:
"Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female,
And said, For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh?
Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder." (KJV)
Notice His words.
"At the beginning."
Jesus was addressing divorce, not answering a direct question about polygamy. We must not pretend otherwise.
But His answer establishes something important about how Christians should understand marriage.
He grounds its meaning in God's creative intention rather than simply treating every arrangement tolerated in Israel's history as the ideal.
In the Greek text of Matthew 19:5, we find:
οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν
Hoi dyo eis sarka mian.
"The two into one flesh."
The word dyo means "two."
Jesus is quoting the creation account and affirming the union of the two.
This does not mean that a single Greek word settles every historical and theological question surrounding polygamy.
But it does mean that the marriage pattern Jesus chose to uphold was the creation pattern of two becoming one flesh.
And suddenly, the question changes.
Instead of asking, "How many wives did Solomon have?"
We begin asking, "What kind of marriage did Jesus hold before His followers?"
That distinction is everything.
Now imagine Sarah.
Not as a stained-glass figure.
Not as a character in a children's Bible lesson.
Imagine her as a woman.
A woman who had waited years for a child.
A woman who knew the ache of unanswered prayers.
A woman who watched time pass while God's promise seemed impossible.
Then came a decision that would fracture her household.
In Genesis 16, Sarah, then called Sarai, gave Hagar, her Egyptian servant, to Abraham in an attempt to obtain a child through her.
It was a decision shaped by desperation, social customs, and the painful reality of infertility in the ancient world.
But when Hagar conceived, the household became a place of conflict.
Genesis 16:4 describes tension between Hagar and Sarai.
Genesis 16:6 tells us that Sarai dealt harshly with Hagar, who fled.
Read that again.
The arrangement did not simply produce another child.
It produced suffering.
And Hagar, a vulnerable servant caught in decisions made by people with power over her, found herself alone in the wilderness.
Yet there, God saw her.
She called Him:
אֵל רֳאִי
El Ro'i.
A Hebrew expression commonly understood as "God who sees me," or "God of seeing" (Genesis 16:13).
What a moment.
In a story often used to debate whether a man may have more than one wife, Scripture draws our attention to a suffering woman whom God does not overlook.
Hagar was not invisible to Him.
Her pain mattered.
Her child mattered.
Her future mattered.
And if we use Abraham's household merely to defend a marriage arrangement while ignoring Hagar's suffering, we have missed something deeply important in the narrative.
God's mercy toward Hagar does not establish that every decision leading to her suffering was righteous.
Neither does Abraham's place in salvation history mean that every action he took reflected God's perfect will.
God's faithfulness is often revealed not through human perfection, but in spite of human failure.
And that should give hope to every reader who carries regrets.
Because perhaps you, too, have made a decision in desperation.
Perhaps you tried to force an answer that God had not yet given.
Perhaps you wounded someone while trying to protect yourself.
Perhaps your family still carries the consequences.
The God who saw Hagar still sees people in pain.
And the God who remained faithful to His promise to Abraham is not defeated by human failure.
But His mercy should never become our excuse to repeat that failure.
Then there was Jacob.
Two sisters.
One husband.
A household full of longing.
Leah wanted to be loved.
Rachel wanted children.
Jacob favored Rachel.
And the competition between the women intensified.
Genesis 29–30 records the heartbreak, rivalry, and painful struggle for affection and motherhood within this family.
Listen to Leah's words after the birth of Reuben:
"Surely the LORD hath looked upon my affliction; now therefore my husband will love me." (Genesis 29:32, KJV)
"Now therefore my husband will love me."
Can you hear the ache?
A woman holding her newborn child, hoping that perhaps this time she will finally receive the love she has been longing for.
This is not a romantic advertisement for polygamy.
It is the account of a family through whom God worked while deep emotional wounds remained.
God brought the twelve tribes of Israel out of Jacob's complicated household.
But divine providence does not mean divine approval of every human choice within that household.
That distinction is crucial.
God can bring redemption out of a broken situation without declaring the brokenness His ideal.
And if you have ever wondered whether your family is too complicated for God's grace, remember Jacob's household.
The Lord's redemptive purposes were not destroyed by their dysfunction.
But neither did their dysfunction become the standard for everyone else.
Now consider David.
A man who worshiped.
A man who repented.
A man who wrote psalms that still comfort wounded souls.
A man whose household also became a place of devastating conflict.
Some defenders of polygamy appeal to 2 Samuel 12:8, where God, through Nathan, speaks of having given David his master's house and wives.
This is one of the more difficult passages in the discussion, and it deserves an honest response.
The verse appears within Nathan's confrontation of David over his adultery with Bathsheba and the killing of Uriah.
The language emphasizes what God had granted David in contrast to David's sinful grasping for what was not his.
It is a serious mistake to ignore this text.
But it is also a mistake to treat the verse as an unrestricted command or universal endorsement of polygamy.
The passage does not instruct Christians to take multiple wives. Nor does it overturn the creation pattern to which Jesus later appealed.
We must allow the text to say what it says, without forcing it to say more.
The Old Testament does contain laws regulating marriages involving multiple wives.
Exodus 21:10 protects a wife's food, clothing, and marital rights if another wife is taken.
Deuteronomy 21:15–17 addresses inheritance when a man has two wives, one loved and one unloved.
These laws are real.
They cannot simply be erased.
But regulation is not the same thing as a declaration that a practice represents God's highest intention.
Biblical law sometimes addresses the realities of a fallen society and places limits on injustice within those realities.
Jesus Himself made a related distinction when explaining that Moses permitted divorce because of the hardness of human hearts, while directing His hearers back to the beginning (Matthew 19:8).
That does not automatically prove every Old Testament allowance functioned identically to the divorce concession.
It does, however, warn us against assuming that every practice addressed by Mosaic law must therefore be God's ideal for all times.
Even Israel's kings were warned.
Deuteronomy 17:17 says of the king:
"Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away." (KJV)
The warning is especially striking when we reach Solomon.
Solomon.
The king renowned for wisdom.
The man who built the temple.
The ruler whose name became associated with extraordinary wealth and splendor.
First Kings 11:3 records that he had seven hundred wives who were princesses and three hundred concubines.
One thousand women.
But the biblical account does not present this as a glorious achievement.
It says his wives turned away his heart.
First Kings 11:4 declares:
"For it came to pass, when Solomon was old, that his wives turned away his heart after other gods: and his heart was not perfect with the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father." (KJV)
We must be precise here.
The passage particularly condemns Solomon's disobedience and idolatry, including the influence of his foreign wives who worshiped other gods.
It should not be reduced to the simplistic claim that every polygamous household inevitably experiences Solomon's exact downfall.
But neither can Solomon's marriages honestly be presented as an uncomplicated biblical endorsement of modern polygamy.
His story is a warning.
And perhaps the most haunting part is this:
A man may possess extraordinary knowledge of God and still fail to obey Him.
A person can quote Scripture and still use it to defend the desires of the heart.
A believer can be admired publicly while privately drifting away from the Lord.
That should humble every one of us.
Because the danger is not merely having the wrong answer to a marriage debate.
The danger is becoming so determined to defend ourselves that we stop allowing Scripture to correct us.
Now we come to the New Testament.
And the question becomes sharper.
What did the apostles teach the churches?
In 1 Corinthians 7:2, Paul writes:
The Greek reads:
ἕκαστος τὴν ἑαυτοῦ γυναῖκα ἐχέτω, καὶ ἑκάστη τὸν ἴδιον ἄνδρα ἐχέτω
Hekastos tēn heautou gynaika echetō, kai hekastē ton idion andra echetō.
The sense is:
"Let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband."
Paul describes marriage in reciprocal terms.
The husband belongs in covenantal faithfulness to his wife, and the wife to her husband.
The surrounding verses emphasize mutual responsibility, mutual consideration, and the shared obligations of marriage.
Paul is not describing a husband collecting wives.
He is instructing husbands and wives in a relationship of mutual marital faithfulness.
In 1 Timothy 3:2, an overseer is required to be:
"the husband of one wife." (KJV)
The Greek expression is:
μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα
Mias gynaikos andra.
Literally, "a man of one woman," commonly expressed as "husband of one wife."
The same expression appears in Titus 1:6, while 1 Timothy 3:12 uses comparable language for deacons.
Scholars discuss whether this phrase primarily emphasizes marital faithfulness, excludes polygamy, addresses remarriage, or combines several concerns.
We should acknowledge that debate rather than pretend every detail is uncontested.
These qualifications directly concern church leaders, so they should not be presented as though they are, by themselves, an explicit universal prohibition addressed to every married Christian.
Yet they fit naturally with the wider New Testament portrayal of marriage as an exclusive covenant between husband and wife.
Then Paul gives us something even deeper.
Ephesians 5:25 says:
"Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it." (KJV)
And in Ephesians 5:31–32, Paul returns to Genesis 2:24 and describes the marriage union as a profound mystery related to Christ and the church.
Here the conversation moves beyond ancient kings and household arrangements.
Marriage is held up as a picture of covenantal, self-giving love.
Christ does not exploit His bride.
He does not abandon her.
He gives Himself for her.
And the Christian husband's calling is not to pursue the greatest number of relationships he can justify.
It is to love with the sacrificial faithfulness modeled by Jesus.
This is why the historic mainstream Christian understanding of marriage is monogamous.
Not because Christians are embarrassed by the Old Testament.
Not because the patriarchs have been erased.
But because the Bible's creation account, Jesus' teaching, and the apostolic vision of marriage together provide a compelling foundation for the covenantal union of one man and one woman.

To be fair, some contemporary defenders of polygamy argue that the Old Testament's regulation of plural marriages, the absence of a single explicit New Testament sentence saying "all polygamy is forbidden," and certain difficult passages leave room for plural marriage.
Those arguments deserve to be examined seriously rather than mocked.
But the absence of one particular prohibition is not sufficient to establish positive Christian authorization.
Christian ethics are not formed merely by searching for everything Scripture does not forbid in one sentence.
They are formed by reading the whole biblical witness in its context, with Jesus Christ at the center.
And that is where the argument for adopting modern polygamy as a Christian ideal becomes deeply unpersuasive.
The Old Testament shows that polygamy existed among God's people. It does not establish that Christians should practice it.
Still, there is another question that deserves compassion.
What about people already living in polygamous families?
What about women and children who would suffer if a husband suddenly abandoned them?
What about converts to Christianity whose family circumstances were established before they came to faith?
These are not abstract theological puzzles.
These are human lives.
Real mothers.
Real children.
Real responsibilities.
Real consequences.
And the church must not answer complex family situations with careless commands that create new injustices.
Repentance never gives someone permission to abandon vulnerable dependents.
The New Testament takes family provision seriously (1 Timothy 5:8), and the Old Testament itself demonstrates concern for the rights of women within existing plural marriages.

How an existing polygamous household should be pastorally addressed can involve difficult questions of civil law, covenantal obligations, protection of women, provision for children, and church membership or leadership.
Faithful Christian communities may differ in their pastoral handling of such circumstances.
But one thing should be clear.
People must never become disposable in the name of defending a theological position.
Jesus calls us to truth.
And He calls us to love.
Not truth without compassion.
Not compassion that refuses truth.
Both.
Always both.
And perhaps you have read this far thinking, "This has nothing to do with me. I am not considering polygamy."
But stay with me.
Because the deepest issue has been following us from the first paragraph.
What do we do when God's Word confronts something we want?
Maybe your struggle is not multiple marriages.
Maybe it is a secret relationship you know dishonors Christ.
Maybe it is pornography that you keep promising to leave behind.
Maybe it is resentment toward your spouse.
Maybe it is emotional unfaithfulness that you have convinced yourself is harmless because nothing physical has happened.
Maybe you have used the failures of biblical characters to excuse your own.
"David sinned."
"Solomon had many wives."
"Abraham made mistakes."
"God still used them."
Yes.
God still used them.
But their stories were never written to make sin comfortable.
They reveal the extraordinary mercy of God toward imperfect people.
And the same grace that forgives us also calls us to change.
Romans 6:1–2 asks:
"What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?
God forbid. How shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein?" (KJV)
Grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
Grace is God's undeserved favor toward sinners, received through faith in Jesus Christ, whose death and resurrection accomplish the salvation we could never earn.
And that grace teaches us to turn away from ungodliness (Titus 2:11–12).
Not because obedience purchases God's love.
But because the love of Christ transforms those who belong to Him.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Jesus did not come merely to win theological arguments.
He came to save sinners.
He came for the ashamed.
For the compromised.
For the self-righteous.
For the wounded.
For the people who know the Bible but have forgotten how to surrender.
For the person whose marriage is falling apart.
For the person whose family history is complicated.
For the believer who has been using Scripture as a shield against conviction.
He came for people who need more than a better argument.
People who need a new heart.
And He gave His life on the cross, bearing our sins, and rose again so that all who repent and trust in Him may receive forgiveness and eternal life.
That is why our message is not simply "Defend monogamy."
Our message is Jesus Christ.
The faithful Bridegroom.
The Savior who keeps His covenant.
The Lord whose mercy is greater than our past and whose authority is greater than our preferences.
Maybe today you need to stop asking, "Can I find a biblical example that makes this acceptable?"
And begin asking, "Lord Jesus, what would faithfulness look like in my life?"
That is a much more difficult prayer.
Because sometimes the truth does not simply correct our theology.
It confronts our desires.
Our relationships.
Our pride.
Our excuses.
But the same Savior who calls us to surrender also welcomes those who come to Him.
He does not promise that repentance will erase every earthly consequence.
He does promise that those who come to Him in faith will not be cast out (John 6:37).
And if your heart is being convicted right now, do not run from Him.
Run to Him.
Tell Him the truth.
Tell Him where you have compromised.
Tell Him where you have been confused.
Tell Him where you have hurt someone.
Tell Him where you need wisdom to make things right.

And if you are already carrying the consequences of complicated relationships, seek wise, biblically grounded pastoral counsel that takes seriously the safety, dignity, and responsibilities owed to everyone involved.
There is grace for the repentant.
There is wisdom for the confused.
There is forgiveness in Christ.
And there is hope for families that desperately need His mercy.
Perhaps this is why the words "From Scandal to Grace" matter so deeply to us at Gospel Warrior.
The Bible is filled with people whose stories could have ended in shame.
Abraham's failures did not cancel God's promise.
Jacob's broken family did not prevent God from forming a nation.
David's terrible sin did not place him beyond the possibility of repentance.
Peter's denial did not become the final chapter of his life.
And Saul the persecutor became Paul the apostle through the astonishing grace of Jesus Christ.
None of these stories make wrongdoing righteous.
They make God's mercy magnificent.
That is the difference.
We do not glorify the scandal.
We glorify the Savior who redeems sinners.
And if this article has challenged something you believed, I want to invite you into an honest conversation.
Not an argument fueled by anger.
Not a contest to see who can quote the most verses.
A conversation that honors Scripture and the people affected by our conclusions.

If you are wrestling with this question, share the passage that troubles you most. If you have a sincere disagreement, explain it with Scripture and humility. If your own family has been affected by complicated marital circumstances, you are welcome to share only what you feel safe sharing.
And if this article has exposed a deeper struggle in your own heart, you can simply comment, "Pray for me."
You do not owe strangers the details of your pain.
But you do not have to pretend that you have everything figured out.
Somewhere on your Facebook friends list is a person who has heard someone use Abraham, David, or Solomon to justify modern polygamy.
Someone who has been confused by the difference between biblical description and biblical approval.
Someone who thinks the Bible contradicts itself.
Someone who may have walked away from Christianity because they believed Christians were hiding difficult passages.
Not to embarrass anyone.
Not to attack another family.
But to open a door for thoughtful, Christ-centered discussion.
Because the next time someone says, "But Solomon had seven hundred wives," you may want to return to the passages we examined and consider the whole biblical picture.
There are too many people forming their understanding of Christianity from isolated verses, viral arguments, and confident voices that have never taken the time to read the surrounding passage.
We want to help change that.
One Scripture.
One honest question.
One wounded heart.
One Gospel-centered conversation at a time.
And if this ministry has strengthened your faith, there is another meaningful way you can stand with us.
Christ has already paid the price for our redemption.
But Scripture does teach that believers may freely and generously support faithful Gospel ministry.
In 2 Corinthians 9:7, Paul writes:
Notice those words.
Not grudgingly.
Not of necessity.
A willing heart.
It should not replace the responsibility to provide for your family, and it should not be confused with a mandatory biblical tithe to a local church.
We encourage believers to remain faithful in supporting their local congregations and the needs of their communities.
But if God has placed Gospel Warrior on your heart as another ministry you would like to support, your partnership would mean a great deal.
To keep pointing people back to Scripture.
To keep proclaiming Jesus Christ.
To keep addressing difficult questions without compromising biblical truth or abandoning compassion.
To keep creating resources for people who are hungry to grow deeper in the faith.
We want these resources to keep reaching people who need them.
It is a small way of expressing gratitude for those who choose to help sustain and expand the work.
You are not less valuable to this ministry.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your thoughtful comments matter.
Your decision to share a biblical message with one person who needs it matters.
The Gospel is not for sale.
And God's grace cannot be purchased.
We simply want to build a community where believers are nourished by Scripture, sharpened in truth, strengthened through prayer, and continually directed toward Jesus Christ.
Because in the end, the question is not whether we can find a famous biblical man who did something we want to do.
The question is whether we are willing to follow the Lord who came to make us new.
Abraham needed grace.
Jacob needed grace.
David needed grace.
Solomon needed grace.
And so do we.
Not grace that excuses every desire.
Grace that forgives.
Grace that restores.
Grace that teaches us to surrender.
Grace that changes the direction of a life.
The Bible does not invite us to build our convictions on the worst decisions of its greatest heroes.
It invites us to place our faith in the one perfect Savior to whom its story ultimately points.
Jesus Christ.
The One who never sinned.
The One who loved sacrificially.
The One who gave Himself for His people.
The One who still calls sinners out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
So when someone asks you again, "If the men of the Old Testament had many wives, why can't Christians today?"
Do not be afraid of the question.
Open the Bible.
Read the stories honestly.
Acknowledge the difficult passages.
Listen to Jesus.
And remember that the greatest example in Scripture is not Abraham, Jacob, David, or Solomon.
It is Christ.
Because the greatest tragedy is not discovering that the heroes of the Bible were broken—it is using their brokenness as an excuse to refuse the healing offered by Jesus.
